text:
Recent work supports history perturbation as a diagnostic of model behavior. Scarcelli et al. (2025) use genetic algorithms to find minimal sequence edits that change recommendations; [TRACE (RecSys 2026)](https://github.com/devUuung/TRACE) targets bringing items into or pushing them out of rankings, including SASRec. These approaches motivate measuring top-10 membership and rank changes rather than only top-1 flips. They explain responses to edited inputs, without establishing effects on real user preferences. [Scarcelli et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606)

Recency deserves a separate control: Petrov et al. (2026) report that simple recency-weighted pairwise models outperform reproduced SASRec/eSASRec models on several benchmarks, with substantial dataset variation. Strong accuracy therefore does not by itself demonstrate higher-order sequence understanding. Compare order shuffling with the last interaction fixed against unrestricted shuffling to distinguish sensitivity to earlier order from dependence on the final item. [Petrov et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19833)

Suggested controlled ablation: remove recent events, remove old interactions isolated in title/description similarity, and remove events from repeatedly represented semantic interests; compare each with repeated random removals matched on count and, where appropriate, age. Treat semantic similarity as an observable proxy, not a preference label. Keep candidates and eligibility masks fixed; report top-10 overlap, original recommendation rank displacement, and paired validation HR@10 changes. Separate position-preserving masking from deletion with sequence compaction. Excess recency sensitivity motivates testing recency weighting; disproportionate isolated-event sensitivity motivates deletion augmentation or consistency regularization; weak shuffle sensitivity motivates a simpler pooled-history baseline. These are hypotheses for validation, not established improvements.
